items.title: Three rhombus tiles
items.source: 2012 Middle Primary Q30 / 2012 Upper Primary Q29
items.prompt: A rhombus-shaped tile is formed by joining two equilateral triangles together. Three of these tiles are combined edge to edge to form a variety of shapes as in the example given. How many different shapes can be formed? (Shapes which are reflections or rotations of other shapes are not considered different.)
items.spoken_script:
Here is the problem. A rhombus-shaped tile is formed by joining two equilateral triangles together. Three of these tiles are combined edge to edge to form a variety of shapes as in the example given. How many different shapes can be formed? (Shapes which are reflections or rotations of other shapes are not considered different.)

Before doing any calculation, say exactly what the question is asking for. Separate the information you are given from the quantity you must find. If there is a picture, use it as a mathematical diagram rather than estimating from how it looks.

Watch out for this common mistake: Different arrangements of internal tile joins can have the same outside shape; those count only once.

A useful first observation is: Draw each rhombus as two equilateral-triangle cells.

Before you continue, think about this: First join two rhombi; up to turning and flipping, there are two different outlines.

Now build the solution in small steps. Pause after any step if you want to reproduce it in your notebook before going on.

Step 1. A rhombus covers two adjacent cells of the equilateral-triangle grid. Two rhombi joined along a full edge give exactly two different outlines when turning and flipping are ignored.

Step 2. For each of those two outlines, place the first triangle of a new rhombus across every exposed edge. Try each possible second triangle beside it, rejecting any overlap with the existing tiles. This checks every way the third rhombus can attach.

Step 3. Compare the resulting six-triangle outlines after all six 60 degrees rotations and after reflection. Keep only one of each matching group; internal tile boundaries do not create a new shape.

Step 4. The nine distinct outlines are shown in the worked gallery. Thus three rhombi can form 9 different shapes.

Check the answer with a different viewpoint. Use three paper rhombi on triangular dot paper. Trace each new outside boundary and compare it with earlier traces by turning the paper over and rotating it.

Final thinking check: When are two drawings counted as the same shape? The question explicitly identifies rotated and reflected copies.

The answer is 9 shapes. Read the original question once more and make sure this is the requested quantity, and that every condition has been checked.

items.title: Catch each green light
items.prompt: Traffic signals at each intersection on a main road all change on the same 2-minute cycle. A taxi driver knows that it is exactly 3.5 km from one intersection to the next. Without breaking the 50 km/h speed limit, what is the highest average speed, in kilometres per hour, he can travel to get to each intersection as it just changes to green?
items.spoken_script:
Here is the problem. Traffic signals at each intersection on a main road all change on the same 2-minute cycle. A taxi driver knows that it is exactly 3.5 km from one intersection to the next. Without breaking the 50 km/h speed limit, what is the highest average speed, in kilometres per hour, he can travel to get to each intersection as it just changes to green?

Before doing any calculation, say exactly what the question is asking for. Separate the information you are given from the quantity you must find. If there is a picture, use it as a mathematical diagram rather than estimating from how it looks.

Watch out for this common mistake: Using the speed limit itself does not guarantee arrival at the beginning of a green phase.

A useful first observation is: Starting on green, the next green starts after a whole number of 2-minute cycles.

Before you continue, think about this: Try travel times 2,4,6, and so on minutes for the 3.5km distance.

Now build the solution in small steps. Pause after any step if you want to reproduce it in your notebook before going on.

Step 1. Arrival at the next green must be after 2, 4, 6, and so on minutes.

Step 2. In 2 minutes the required speed is 3.5 times 30=105 km/h; too fast.

Step 3. In 4 minutes it is 3.5 times 15=52.5 km/h; still too fast.

Step 4. In 6 minutes it is 3.5 times 10=35 km/h, which is permitted.

Step 5. Longer travel times give lower average speeds, so 35 km/h is the largest possible.

Check the answer with a different viewpoint. At 50 km/h the trip takes 4.2 minutes. The first allowed 2-minute multiple at least that large is 6 minutes.

Final thinking check: Why does the first permitted travel time give the highest permitted speed? Speed is distance divided by time. Among allowed times, the shortest gives the largest speed.

The answer is 35 km/h. Read the original question once more and make sure this is the requested quantity, and that every condition has been checked.

items.title: Add all the digits
items.prompt: Rani wrote down the numbers from 1 to 100 on a piece of paper and then correctly added up all the individual digits of the numbers. What sum did she obtain?
items.spoken_script:
Here is the problem. Rani wrote down the numbers from 1 to 100 on a piece of paper and then correctly added up all the individual digits of the numbers. What sum did she obtain?

Before doing any calculation, say exactly what the question is asking for. Separate the information you are given from the quantity you must find. If there is a picture, use it as a mathematical diagram rather than estimating from how it looks.

Watch out for this common mistake: Adding the numbers 1 to 100 is different from adding their individual digits.

A useful first observation is: Look at the digits in the units column for 00 to 99.

Before you continue, think about this: Each digit occurs equally often in each of the two columns. Leading zeroes add nothing to a digit sum.

Now build the solution in small steps. Pause after any step if you want to reproduce it in your notebook before going on.

Step 1. First consider 00 to 99. In the units column, each digit 0 to 9 occurs ten times, contributing 10 times 45=450.

Step 2. The tens column contributes the same 450.

Step 3. Adding leading zeroes or including 00 changes no digit sum, so 1 to 99 also contributes 900.

Step 4. The number 100 contributes 1+0+0=1. The total is 901.

Check the answer with a different viewpoint. Pair numbers 1 and 98, 2 and 97, and so on; use a place-value table to handle the endpoints carefully.

Final thinking check: How many times does 7 appear in the tens column of 00 to 99? It appears in 70,71, and so on ,79: ten numbers.

The answer is 901. Read the original question once more and make sure this is the requested quantity, and that every condition has been checked.

items.title: Opposite-face products
items.prompt: This cube has a different whole number on each face, and has the property that whichever pair of opposite faces is chosen, the two numbers multiply to give the same result. What is the smallest possible total of all 6 numbers on the cube?
items.spoken_script:
Here is the problem. This cube has a different whole number on each face, and has the property that whichever pair of opposite faces is chosen, the two numbers multiply to give the same result. What is the smallest possible total of all 6 numbers on the cube?

Before doing any calculation, say exactly what the question is asking for. Separate the information you are given from the quantity you must find. If there is a picture, use it as a mathematical diagram rather than estimating from how it looks.

Watch out for this common mistake: Being a common multiple is necessary but not sufficient: every one of the six labels must also be different.

A useful first observation is: Call the common opposite-face product P. What are the three hidden numbers in terms of P?

Before you continue, think about this: P must be divisible by 6,9 and 12. Start with their least common multiple.

Now build the solution in small steps. Pause after any step if you want to reproduce it in your notebook before going on.

Step 1. The hidden opposites are P/6, P/9, P/12, so P is divisible by 6, 9 and 12. Their least common multiple is 36.

Step 2. P=0 would put 0 on all three hidden faces, which is forbidden. Try positive multiples of 36.

Step 3. For P=36 the hidden faces are 6, 4, 3; 6 repeats. For 72 they are 12, 8, 6; 12 and 6 repeat. For 108 they are 18, 12, 9; 12 and 9 repeat. For 144 they are 24, 16, 12; 12 repeats.

Step 4. For P=180 the hidden faces are 30, 20, 15. All six numbers are different.

Step 5. Their total is 6+9+12+30+20+15=92. Larger common products increase all hidden numbers, so cannot improve the sum.

Check the answer with a different viewpoint. Use a table with common product and all six face values. Keep the first row with six distinct entries.

Final thinking check: Why is common product 36 rejected? The opposite of 6 would be 36 divided by 6=6, violating the condition that all six numbers differ.

The answer is 92. Read the original question once more and make sure this is the requested quantity, and that every condition has been checked.

items.title: Ages five years later
items.prompt: Andrew has two children, David and Helen. The sum of their three ages is 49. David’s age is three times that of Helen. In 5 years time, Andrew’s age will be three times David’s age. What is the product of their ages now?
items.spoken_script:
Here is the problem. Andrew has two children, David and Helen. The sum of their three ages is 49. David’s age is three times that of Helen. In 5 years time, Andrew’s age will be three times David’s age. What is the product of their ages now?

Before doing any calculation, say exactly what the question is asking for. Separate the information you are given from the quantity you must find. If there is a picture, use it as a mathematical diagram rather than estimating from how it looks.

Watch out for this common mistake: In five years David will be 3h+5, not 3(h+5): the present ratio does not remain constant.

A useful first observation is: Use Helen’s age as one part. David is three such parts.

Before you continue, think about this: Use the total 49 to express Andrew’s age.

Now build the solution in small steps. Pause after any step if you want to reproduce it in your notebook before going on.

Step 1. Let Helen be h years old. David is 3 h and Andrew is 49 minus 4 h.

Step 2. Five years later their ages are h+5, 3 h+5 and 54 minus 4 h.

Step 3. The future clue says 54 minus 4 h=3(3 h+5)=9 h+15.

Step 4. Thus 13 h=39 and h=3. David is 9 and Andrew 37.

Step 5. The product now is 3 times 9 times 37=999. Check: in five years Andrew is 42 and David 14, and 42=3 times 14.

Check the answer with a different viewpoint. Try positive whole-number Helen ages, using the current total to find Andrew and testing the future condition.

Final thinking check: If David is 3h now, how old is he in five years? Five years adds 5 to each person’s age, regardless of their present ratio.

The answer is 999. Read the original question once more and make sure this is the requested quantity, and that every condition has been checked.

items.title: The tablet bottle
items.prompt: I take 2 vitamin C tablets every day. If I increase my dose to 3 tablets a day, a full bottle would last 8 days less. How many tablets are in a full bottle?
items.spoken_script:
Here is the problem. I take 2 vitamin C tablets every day. If I increase my dose to 3 tablets a day, a full bottle would last 8 days less. How many tablets are in a full bottle?

Before doing any calculation, say exactly what the question is asking for. Separate the information you are given from the quantity you must find. If there is a picture, use it as a mathematical diagram rather than estimating from how it looks.

Watch out for this common mistake: The 8-day difference is not the bottle’s full duration at either rate.

A useful first observation is: Consider a group of 6 tablets.

Before you continue, think about this: At 2 per day it lasts 3 days; at 3 per day it lasts 2 days.

Now build the solution in small steps. Pause after any step if you want to reproduce it in your notebook before going on.

Step 1. Every group of 6 tablets lasts 3 days at 2 tablets a day, but 2 days at 3 tablets a day.

Step 2. So each group of 6 produces a difference of 1 day. An 8-day difference requires 8 such groups.

Step 3. The bottle contains 8 times 6 = 48 tablets. Check:48 divided by 2 = 24 days and 48 divided by 3 = 16 days, a difference of 8.

Check the answer with a different viewpoint. If there are N tablets, N/2 minus N/3 = N/6 = 8, so N = 48.

Final thinking check: How long do 6 tablets last at 2 per day? 6 divided by 2 = 3 days.

The answer is 48 tablets. Read the original question once more and make sure this is the requested quantity, and that every condition has been checked.

items.title: Four shaded triangles
items.prompt: Each side of the large square is 30 cm. Its side midpoints are joined to corners as shown. What is the total shaded area, in square centimetres?
items.spoken_script:
Here is the problem. Each side of the large square is 30 cm. Its side midpoints are joined to corners as shown. What is the total shaded area, in square centimetres?

Before doing any calculation, say exactly what the question is asking for. Separate the information you are given from the quantity you must find. If there is a picture, use it as a mathematical diagram rather than estimating from how it looks.

Watch out for this common mistake: The tip is not halfway across the half-side; measuring the picture or assuming height 7.5 cm gives the wrong area.

A useful first observation is: The four shaded triangles are congruent by quarter-turn symmetry.

Before you continue, think about this: Focus on the top triangle. Its top-edge base is 15 cm.

Now build the solution in small steps. Pause after any step if you want to reproduce it in your notebook before going on.

Step 1. The four shaded triangles are congruent, so find one area and multiply by 4. The top triangle has base 15 cm, half the square’s 30 cm side.

Step 2. Let its tip be h cm below the top edge and x cm right of the left edge. The line from the top midpoint to the bottom-right corner moves right 1 for every 2 down, so x = 15 + h/2.

Step 3. The other line goes from the left midpoint to the top-right corner, moving right 2 for every 1 up. Its tip is 15 minus h cm above the left midpoint, so x = 2 (15 minus h) = 30 minus 2 h.

Step 4. Equating gives 15 + h/2 = 30 minus 2 h, so (5/2)h = 15 and h = 6. One area is (15 times 6)/2 = 45 cm squared; all four total 4 times 45 = 180 cm squared.

Check the answer with a different viewpoint. Take coordinates from the bottom-left corner. The top tip is the intersection of y = 60 minus 2 x and y = 15 + x/2, giving (18,24). Its distance below the top is 6 cm.

Final thinking check: Why can you multiply one shaded triangle’s area by 4? The midpoint-to-corner construction repeats exactly after a 90 degrees rotation.

The answer is 180 cm². Read the original question once more and make sure this is the requested quantity, and that every condition has been checked.

items.title: Repeated digits
items.prompt: Starting at 100 and going through to 999, how many numbers have two or more digits the same?
items.spoken_script:
Here is the problem. Starting at 100 and going through to 999, how many numbers have two or more digits the same?

Before doing any calculation, say exactly what the question is asking for. Separate the information you are given from the quantity you must find. If there is a picture, use it as a mathematical diagram rather than estimating from how it looks.

Watch out for this common mistake: Zero is allowed in the tens and units places. Counting the distinct digits as 9 times 8 times 7 would wrongly exclude it.

A useful first observation is: It is easier to count numbers whose three digits are all different.

Before you continue, think about this: There are 9 choices for the hundreds digit, then 9 for the tens digit, then 8 for the units digit.

Now build the solution in small steps. Pause after any step if you want to reproduce it in your notebook before going on.

Step 1. There are 999 minus 100 + 1 = 900 three-digit numbers.

Step 2. For all digits to be different, the hundreds digit has 9 choices (1 to 9). The tens digit has 9 choices (0 to 9 except the hundreds digit), and the units digit has 8 choices left.

Step 3. There are 9 times 9 times 8 = 648 numbers with no repeated digit.

Step 4. All other numbers have at least two equal digits:900 minus 648 = 252.

Check the answer with a different viewpoint. For each fixed hundreds digit, count three events: tens equals hundreds (10 choices), units equals hundreds (10), or tens equals units (10). Each pairwise overlap and the triple overlap is the all-equal number. Inclusion to exclusion gives 30 minus 3 + 1 = 28; across nine hundreds digits this is 9 times 28 = 252.

Final thinking check: Why are there 9 choices for the tens digit? There are 10 possible digits including 0, and exactly one has already been used.

The answer is 252 numbers. Read the original question once more and make sure this is the requested quantity, and that every condition has been checked.

items.title: Three numbers divisible by three
items.source: 2013 Middle Primary Q29 / 2013 Upper Primary Q27
items.prompt: In how many ways can three different numbers be selected from the numbers 1 to 12, so that their sum can be exactly divided by 3?
items.spoken_script:
Here is the problem. In how many ways can three different numbers be selected from the numbers 1 to 12, so that their sum can be exactly divided by 3?

Before doing any calculation, say exactly what the question is asking for. Separate the information you are given from the quantity you must find. If there is a picture, use it as a mathematical diagram rather than estimating from how it looks.

Watch out for this common mistake: The order of the chosen numbers does not create a new selection, so do not multiply the 012 count by 6.

A useful first observation is: Group 1 to 12 by their remainders when divided by 3. Each group contains 4 numbers.

Before you continue, think about this: Three remainders total a multiple of 3 if all are equal or if they are 0,1 and 2.

Now build the solution in small steps. Pause after any step if you want to reproduce it in your notebook before going on.

Step 1. The remainder groups are 0:{3,6,9,12},1:{1,4,7,10}, and 2:{2,5,8,11}.

Step 2. A valid selection uses remainder pattern 000,111,222 or 012. These are the only ways three remainders can sum to a multiple of 3.

Step 3. For any all-equal pattern, choose 3 of the group’s 4 numbers:4 possibilities, found by choosing the one omitted. The three groups give 3 times 4 = 12 selections.

Step 4. For 012, choose one number from each group:4 times 4 times 4 = 64. Total 12 + 64 = 76 selections.

Check the answer with a different viewpoint. List all 220 three-element subsets of 1 to 12 and retain sums divisible by 3; exactly 76 remain.

Final thinking check: Which remainder pattern does NOT make a divisible-by-3 sum? 0 + 0 + 1 leaves remainder 1, while the other sums are 3.

The answer is 76 selections. Read the original question once more and make sure this is the requested quantity, and that every condition has been checked.

items.title: Carrying the library books
items.source: 2013 Middle Primary Q30 / 2013 Upper Primary Q28
items.prompt: Adam, Barney and Joe carry 999 books out of the library. Adam works for 3 hours, Barney works for 4 hours and Joe works for 5 hours. They work at different speeds, with Adam carrying 5 books for every 3 books Barney carries and every 2 books Joe carries. How many books did Adam carry?
items.spoken_script:
Here is the problem. Adam, Barney and Joe carry 999 books out of the library. Adam works for 3 hours, Barney works for 4 hours and Joe works for 5 hours. They work at different speeds, with Adam carrying 5 books for every 3 books Barney carries and every 2 books Joe carries. How many books did Adam carry?

Before doing any calculation, say exactly what the question is asking for. Separate the information you are given from the quantity you must find. If there is a picture, use it as a mathematical diagram rather than estimating from how it looks.

Watch out for this common mistake: Sharing 999 directly in the rate ratio 5:3:2 ignores that they worked for different durations.

A useful first observation is: The 5:3:2 ratio describes equal amounts of time, not their final totals.

Before you continue, think about this: Multiply each rate part by that person’s working hours.

Now build the solution in small steps. Pause after any step if you want to reproduce it in your notebook before going on.

Step 1. Their carrying rates are in the ratio Adam:Barney:Joe = 5:3:2.

Step 2. Multiply by their hours: Adam 5 times 3 = 15 parts, Barney 3 times 4 = 12 parts, Joe 2 times 5 = 10 parts.

Step 3. The total is 15 + 12 + 10 = 37 parts, so one part represents 999 divided by 37 = 27 books.

Step 4. Adam carries 15 times 27 = 405 books. Barney carries 324 and Joe 270; together they carry 999.

Check the answer with a different viewpoint. Let hourly rates be 5 k,3 k,2 k. Then their total is (3 times 5 + 4 times 3 + 5 times 2)k = 37 k = 999, so k 27.

Final thinking check: What is Adam’s share of the total-work ratio? His rate weight 5 is multiplied by his 3 working hours.

The answer is 405 books. Read the original question once more and make sure this is the requested quantity, and that every condition has been checked.

items.title: The right price per kilogram
items.prompt: Dried dog food is available in three sizes: 1 kg bags, which cost $6; 3 kg bags, which cost $15; and 8 kg bags, which cost $25. What is the smallest number of bags you can buy such that the average price per kilogram is exactly $4?
items.spoken_script:
Here is the problem. Dried dog food is available in three sizes: 1 kg bags, which cost $6; 3 kg bags, which cost $15; and 8 kg bags, which cost $25. What is the smallest number of bags you can buy such that the average price per kilogram is exactly $4?

Before doing any calculation, say exactly what the question is asking for. Separate the information you are given from the quantity you must find. If there is a picture, use it as a mathematical diagram rather than estimating from how it looks.

Watch out for this common mistake: Average price per kilogram is total cost divided by total weight, not the average of the three displayed bag prices.

A useful first observation is: Compare each bag’s price with what the same weight would cost at$4/kg.

Before you continue, think about this: Some bags are above the target and one type is below. Their cost differences must balance.

Now build the solution in small steps. Pause after any step if you want to reproduce it in your notebook before going on.

Step 1. At $4/kg the three bag sizes would cost $4,$12,$32. Their actual deviations are+$2,+$3, minus $7.

Step 2. At least one 8 kg bag is needed because the other types are above $4/kg.

Step 3. With fewer than four bags, if there is one 8 kg bag there are at most two other bags, giving at most $6 surplus, less than $7. If there are two or more 8 kg bags, at most one other bag gives at most $3 surplus against a discount of at least $14. No solution uses three or fewer bags.

Step 4. Two 1 kg bags and one 3 kg bag give surplus 2+2+3=7, balancing one 8 kg bag.

Step 5. These four bags weigh 13 kg and cost $52. Since 52 divided by 13=4, the minimum is 4 bags.

Check the answer with a different viewpoint. List all combinations of one, two and three bags to rule them out; then find 2 small, 1 medium, 1 large.

Final thinking check: What is the target cost of an 8kg bag at$4/kg? 8 times 4=$32, so the actual$25 price supplies a$7 discount to balance surplus costs elsewhere.

The answer is 4 bags. Read the original question once more and make sure this is the requested quantity, and that every condition has been checked.

items.title: Ascending then descending
items.prompt: Find the largest 3-digit number, with no two digits the same and with its digits in ascending order, which when multiplied by 5 has its digits in descending order?
items.spoken_script:
Here is the problem. Find the largest 3-digit number, with no two digits the same and with its digits in ascending order, which when multiplied by 5 has its digits in descending order?

Before doing any calculation, say exactly what the question is asking for. Separate the information you are given from the quantity you must find. If there is a picture, use it as a mathematical diagram rather than estimating from how it looks.

Watch out for this common mistake: A larger first digit in the product is not enough: every successive digit must be strictly smaller.

A useful first observation is: What is the largest three-digit number with strictly increasing digits? Use it to bound the product.

Before you continue, think about this: If the product has four digits, what strictly decreasing four-digit numbers could lie below that bound?

Now build the solution in small steps. Pause after any step if you want to reproduce it in your notebook before going on.

Step 1. Any increasing three-digit number is at most 789, so its product by 5 is at most 3945.

Step 2. If the original is at least 200, the product has four digits. A strictly decreasing four-digit number below 4000 must be 3210: four different decreasing digits need to start at least 3.

Step 3. But 3210 divided by 5=642, whose digits are not increasing, so the original must be below 200.

Step 4. The largest increasing possibilities below 200 in descending order are 189, 179, 178, 169, 168.

Step 5. Their products are 945, 895, 890, 845, 840. The first strictly decreasing product is 840, so the largest original is 168.

Check the answer with a different viewpoint. List the increasing three-digit candidates, multiply each by 5 and compare the product’s adjacent digits.

Final thinking check: Which product has strictly decreasing digits? 8>4>0. The other products rise at least once.

The answer is 168. Read the original question once more and make sure this is the requested quantity, and that every condition has been checked.

items.title: Keep the game close
items.prompt: A hockey game between two teams is ‘relatively close’ if the number of goals scored by the two teams never differ by more than two. In how many ways can the first 12 goals of a game be scored if the game is ‘relatively close’?
items.spoken_script:
Here is the problem. A hockey game between two teams is ‘relatively close’ if the number of goals scored by the two teams never differ by more than two. In how many ways can the first 12 goals of a game be scored if the game is ‘relatively close’?

Before doing any calculation, say exactly what the question is asking for. Separate the information you are given from the quantity you must find. If there is a picture, use it as a mathematical diagram rather than estimating from how it looks.

Watch out for this common mistake: Checking only the final score counts orders that had an illegal lead earlier in the game.

A useful first observation is: After an odd number of goals, what can the score difference be?

Before you continue, think about this: From a lead of 1, list the allowed orders of the next two goals. One of the four possible pairs is forbidden.

Now build the solution in small steps. Pause after any step if you want to reproduce it in your notebook before going on.

Step 1. There are 2 choices for the first goal: team A or team B.

Step 2. After any odd number of goals, one team leads by 1. For the next pair, if A leads, the permitted orders are AB, BA, BB. AA would create a forbidden lead of 3. If B leads, the symmetric three choices apply.

Step 3. Each permitted pair ends with a difference of 1 again, so this rule can be repeated independently for five pairs, covering goals 2 through 11.

Step 4. From the resulting difference of 1, either team may score goal 12, leaving difference 0 or 2.

Step 5. Total orders=2 times 3 times 3 times 3 times 3 times 3 times 2=972.

Check the answer with a different viewpoint. Build a table of counts for differences minus 2, minus 1, 0, 1, 2. Each entry receives the previous row’s neighboring entries; delete moves outside the allowed interval. At 12 goals the counts are 243, 0, 486, 0, 243.

Final thinking check: If A leads by 1, which next two-goal order breaks the rule? AA changes the lead from 1 to 2 and then 3, exceeding the permitted difference.

The answer is 972 orders. Read the original question once more and make sure this is the requested quantity, and that every condition has been checked.

items.title: Make the largest number
items.prompt: Six different whole numbers, chosen from the numbers from 1 to 100, add up to 100. What is the greatest possible value of the largest of these numbers?
items.spoken_script:
Here is the problem. Six different whole numbers, chosen from the numbers from 1 to 100, add up to 100. What is the greatest possible value of the largest of these numbers?

Before doing any calculation, say exactly what the question is asking for. Separate the information you are given from the quantity you must find. If there is a picture, use it as a mathematical diagram rather than estimating from how it looks.

Watch out for this common mistake: Using five copies of 1 ignores the requirement that all six numbers are different.

A useful first observation is: The total is fixed, so make the other five numbers as small as possible.

Before you continue, think about this: The five numbers must be different and at least 1. Which five have the smallest sum?

Now build the solution in small steps. Pause after any step if you want to reproduce it in your notebook before going on.

Step 1. To make the largest number as large as possible, minimise the sum of the other five.

Step 2. The smallest five different numbers allowed are 1,2,3,4,5, with sum 15.

Step 3. The remaining number is 100 minus 15=85. It is different from the other five and lies between 1 and 100, so 85 is attainable and maximal.

Check the answer with a different viewpoint. If the largest were 86 or more, the other five would total 14 or less, below their minimum possible total 15.

Final thinking check: Why do we use 1,2,3,4,5 for the other numbers? Leaving the smallest possible total for the other five leaves the greatest possible remainder.

The answer is 85. Read the original question once more and make sure this is the requested quantity, and that every condition has been checked.

items.title: Palindromes between 100 and 300
items.prompt: A number is palindromic if it reads the same forwards as backwards. For example, 686 is palindromic. How many numbers from 100 to 300 are palindromic?
items.spoken_script:
Here is the problem. A number is palindromic if it reads the same forwards as backwards. For example, 686 is palindromic. How many numbers from 100 to 300 are palindromic?

Before doing any calculation, say exactly what the question is asking for. Separate the information you are given from the quantity you must find. If there is a picture, use it as a mathematical diagram rather than estimating from how it looks.

Watch out for this common mistake: Forgetting that the middle digit may be 0 loses 101 and 202.

A useful first observation is: A three-digit palindrome has the same first and last digit.

Before you continue, think about this: Its hundreds digit can be 1 or 2. What can the middle digit be?

Now build the solution in small steps. Pause after any step if you want to reproduce it in your notebook before going on.

Step 1. Write a three-digit palindrome as ABA: its first and last digits agree.

Step 2. Between 100 and 300, A can only be 1 or 2;300 itself is not a palindrome.

Step 3. For each A, B can be any digit 0 to 9, giving 10 choices. Thus 2 times 10=20 palindromes.

Check the answer with a different viewpoint. List 101,111, and so on ,191 and 202,212, and so on ,292: two lists of 10.

Final thinking check: Can the middle digit be 0? 101 and 202 are valid three-digit palindromes.

The answer is 20 numbers. Read the original question once more and make sure this is the requested quantity, and that every condition has been checked.

items.title: The rowing fleet
items.prompt: A group of 64 students went rowing. They were given 12 rowing boats, each boat either large or small. The large boats each carried 6 students and the small ones 4 students. How many large boats were they given?
items.spoken_script:
Here is the problem. A group of 64 students went rowing. They were given 12 rowing boats, each boat either large or small. The large boats each carried 6 students and the small ones 4 students. How many large boats were they given?

Step 4. The four ages are 4,7,8,9, with sum 28.

Here is the problem. Today my three cousins multiplied their ages together and it came to 2016. This day last year their ages multiplied to 1377. When they multiplied their ages together 2 years ago today, what was their answer?

Step 1. Factor last year’s product:1377=3⁴ times 17. A last-year age containing 17 must be 17,51,153,459 or 1377. The corresponding current ages are 18,52,154,460,1378. Only 18 divides 2016, so one cousin is 18 now.

Step 4. The current ages are 4,18,28. Two years ago they were 2,16,26, whose product is 2 times 16 times 26=832.

Final thinking check: What does (x minus 1)(y minus 1)=81 tell us when xy=112? Expanding gives 81=112 minus x minus y+1, hence x+y=32.

The answer is 832. Read the original question once more and make sure this is the requested quantity, and that every condition has been checked.
